Wretchedness
RECH-ed-nes
n. (misery; Moses' word for what he asked God not to make him watch)
From Old English wrecca, an exile or outcast. At Numbers 11:15 it renders Hebrew ra'ah, evil or calamity — Moses asking not to see his own.

Biblical Definition

Moses has been given a people who weep for flesh, and his prayer is one of the bluntest in the Bible: And if thou deal thus with me, kill me, I pray thee, out of hand, if I have found favour in thy sight; and let me not see my wretchedness. He has already said I am not able to bear all this people alone, because it is too heavy for me, and before that had asked God why the burden was laid on him at all. This is the meekest man in all the earth asking to be killed rather than to go on, and the Holy Ghost preserved it without editing.

What God does with it is the point. There is no rebuke. He tells Moses to gather seventy elders, and says, I will take of the spirit which is upon thee, and will put it upon them; and they shall bear the burden of the people with thee, that thou bear it not thyself alone. The answer to a crushed leader is not a scolding and not a miracle but seventy men. Paul's use of the same word in Romans 7 shows how far it reaches: O wretched man that I am! who shall deliver me from the body of this death? — and there too the cry is answered in the next breath rather than left hanging: I thank God through Jesus Christ our Lord. Scripture lets its best men say the worst thing they are feeling, and then answers it.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828): extreme misery or unhappiness; a state of distress or affliction.

expand to see more

WRETCHEDNESS, n. Extreme misery or unhappiness, either from want or from pain of body or anguish of mind.

WRETCH, n. A miserable person; one sunk in vice or degradation; one deeply afflicted.

MISERY, n. Great unhappiness; extreme pain of body or mind; wretchedness; distress.

BURDEN, n. That which is borne or carried; a load; that which is grievous, wearisome or oppressive.

ELDER, n. One who is older; in Scripture, a person who on account of age is selected to be a ruler or officer.

Key Scripture

Numbers 11:15 — "And if thou deal thus with me, kill me, I pray thee, out of hand, if I have found favour in thy sight; and let me not see my wretchedness."

Numbers 11:14 — "I am not able to bear all this people alone, because it is too heavy for me."

Numbers 11:17 — "And I will come down and talk with thee there: and I will take of the spirit which is upon thee, and will put it upon them; and they shall bear the burden of the people with thee, that thou bear it not thyself alone."

Romans 7:24 — "O wretched man that I am! who shall deliver me from the body of this death?"

Modern Corruption

Despair in a believer is met with rebuke or with silence, when Scripture records it from Moses, Elijah, Job, Jeremiah and Paul, and shows God answering rather than scolding.

expand to see more

A Christian who says what Moses said in Numbers 11 will generally be corrected before he is heard. Yet the Bible preserves the sentence, and preserves Elijah under the juniper asking to die, and Job cursing his day, and Jeremiah wishing he had not been born, and Jonah saying it was better for him to die than to live. In not one of these cases is the man rebuked for the words. Elijah is given sleep and food and then a quiet voice; Job is answered out of the whirlwind and then vindicated; Moses is given seventy men. God's treatment of His exhausted servants is the strongest argument in Scripture against the reflex to hush them.

That does not make despair true. Moses was wrong about his situation, and Paul's O wretched man that I am is followed immediately by I thank God through Jesus Christ our Lord. But the order matters, and the church routinely reverses it: the answer is supplied before the cry has been allowed. Numbers 11 shows the better pattern — let the man say it, in full, to God; and then do what God did, which was to lift the actual weight off him by putting other shoulders under it.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew ra'ah (H7451), evil, calamity, misery; massa (H4853), a burden; Greek talaiporos (G5005), wretched.

expand to see more

Hebrew ra'ah (H7451) — evil, distress, calamity; rendered wretchedness in Moses' prayer.

Hebrew massa (H4853) — a burden, a load; what he said was too heavy for him.

Hebrew ruach (H7307) — spirit; taken of that which was on Moses and put on seventy.

Greek talaiporos (G5005) — wretched, enduring hardship; Paul's cry in Romans 7:24.

Greek rhuomai (G4506) — to draw to oneself, to deliver; who shall deliver me?

Usage

"“let me not see my wretchedness” — the meekest man in the earth, asking to die."

"“that thou bear it not thyself alone” — the answer was seventy men."

"“O wretched man that I am!” — and the thanksgiving in the next verse."
